misconceptions.description: Misses an object or counts one twice when counting, so the count is one out.
Does not see that the last number said when counting is how many there are; counts again or gives the whole counting sequence.
Mixes up the number before and the number after, or one more and one less.
Does not cross a tens boundary correctly when counting, e.g. 28, 29, 20 or 39, 40, 50.
Thinks a group that is spread out, or takes up more space, has more objects.
Confuses teen numbers with multiples of ten or reverses their digits, e.g. 14 with 40 or 41.
Thinks only numerals can show an amount, not marks, pictures, fingers or objects.
Thinks a different arrangement of the same objects is a different number.
Adds the whole and a part instead of finding the missing part.
Counts on or back in ones instead of in the step asked for (2s, 5s, 10s and so on).
Changes the wrong digit when finding one more, ten more and so on, e.g. one more than 34 is 44.
Counts the marks on a number line instead of the jumps between them, so is one out, or ignores the scale.
Gives a digit's face value instead of its value from its place, e.g. says the 4 in 47 is worth 4.
Writes the digits in the wrong order, e.g. 3 tens and 5 ones as 53.
Reads or writes < and > the wrong way round.
Compares numbers by their ones digits, or by the number of digits shown, rather than from the largest place.
Writes numbers as they are said, e.g. sixty-three as 603 or one hundred and five as 1005.
Gives a digit the value of the place next to its own, e.g. says the 3 in 4372 is worth 3000 or 30.
Leaves out zero as a placeholder, e.g. writes 3 hundreds and 5 ones as 35.
Compares the first digits without checking how many digits each number has, e.g. thinks 9856 is greater than 10 002.
Rounds down whatever the next digit is, or simply cuts off the digits.
Rounds a number exactly halfway down instead of up, e.g. rounds 250 to 200.
Rounds to the wrong place, e.g. to the nearest 10 when asked for the nearest 100.
Counts back through zero as 2, 1, 0, 1, 2, or drops the minus sign.
Thinks a negative number with a bigger digit is greater, e.g. that −8 is greater than −3.
Adds every Roman numeral, so reads IV as 6 or XC as 110, instead of subtracting a smaller numeral before a larger one.
Multiplies when it should divide by 10, 100 or 1000, or the reverse, so the digits move the wrong way.
Multiplies a decimal by 10, 100 or 1000 by writing zeros on the end, e.g. 3.4 × 10 = 3.40.
Thinks a decimal with more digits is bigger, e.g. that 0.35 is greater than 0.4.
Treats subtracting a negative number as subtracting a positive one, e.g. 5 − (−3) = 2.
Gets the sign wrong when multiplying or dividing with negative numbers.
Puts the decimal point in the wrong place after multiplying or dividing decimals.
Adds (or subtracts) the numerators and the denominators separately, e.g. 1/2 + 1/3 = 2/5.
Multiplies two numbers to find their lowest common multiple even when they share a factor.
Mixes up the highest common factor and the lowest common multiple.
Includes numbers that are not prime in a prime factorisation, or counts 1 as a prime.
Works from left to right instead of following the order of operations (brackets, powers, × and ÷, then + and −).
Uses the wrong inverse fact, e.g. from a ÷ b = c concludes that a × c = b.
Multiplies the base by the index instead of multiplying the base by itself, e.g. 2⁵ = 10.
Halves a number instead of taking its square root, or divides by 3 instead of taking its cube root.
Treats a rounded decimal as the exact value of a root, e.g. √2 = 1.414.
Counts leading zeros as significant figures.
Rounds to decimal places when asked for significant figures, or the reverse.
Gets the ends of an error interval wrong, e.g. includes the upper bound or uses the wrong half-unit.
Misreads a calculator display in money, e.g. reads 3.5 as £3.05.
Rounds a calculator answer without thinking about the context, e.g. books 4 coaches for 125 people when each holds 30.
Gets the power of ten wrong in standard form, often by counting digits instead of places moved.
Compares numbers in standard form by their first number, ignoring the powers of ten.
Multiplies the powers of ten instead of adding them when multiplying in standard form, or adds them when dividing.
Thinks there is no number between two close decimals or fractions.
Gives the negative of a number as its reciprocal, e.g. the reciprocal of 4 is −4.
Misses or repeats arrangements when listing systematically, or adds the number of choices instead of multiplying.
Reads a negative index as making the number negative, e.g. 2⁻³ = −8 instead of 1/8.
Thinks any number to the power 0 is 0, rather than 1.
Writes a recurring decimal as if it stopped, e.g. 1/3 = 0.3, or thinks every fraction gives a terminating decimal.
Uses the upper bound of both numbers to find the upper bound of a division, instead of dividing the upper bound by the lower bound.
Thinks increasing and then decreasing by the same percentage gets back to the start.
Counts the starting number when counting on or back, so the answer is one out, e.g. 5 + 3 counted as 5, 6, 7.
Reads = as "the answer comes next" rather than "is the same as", e.g. writes 7 in 3 + 4 = ? + 5.
Thinks subtraction can be done in either order, like addition, e.g. 3 − 8 = 5.
Uses the same operation instead of the inverse to find a missing number or check an answer, e.g. ? − 6 = 9 gives 3.
Picks the operation from a key word rather than the structure of the problem, e.g. adds because the question says "more".
Takes the smaller digit from the larger in each column instead of exchanging, e.g. 52 − 27 = 35.
Forgets to carry the exchanged ten (or hundred) into the next column when adding.
Lines numbers up from the left instead of by place value, e.g. 345 + 27 worked as 345 + 270.
Stops after the first step of a problem that needs two or more steps.
Adds instead of multiplying, e.g. 4 groups of 3, or 3 times as many as 4, gives 7.
Gives the next or previous multiple when recalling a times-table fact, e.g. 7 × 8 = 48.
Thinks division can be done in either order, like multiplication, e.g. 3 ÷ 12 = 4.
Forgets to add the carried digit in a written multiplication.
Multiplies only some of the parts after partitioning, e.g. 23 × 45 worked as 20 × 40 + 3 × 5.
Forgets that the tens digit is worth tens in long multiplication, so leaves out the zero placeholder.
Drops the remainder from one digit instead of carrying it to the next in short division.
Gives the quotient without thinking about the remainder in context, e.g. 4 boxes when 30 cakes go into boxes of 8.
Writes the remainder as the digits after a decimal point, e.g. 17 ÷ 5 = 3 r 2 written as 3.2.
Mixes up multiplying by 0 and by 1, e.g. 7 × 0 = 7 or 7 × 1 = 1.
Miscounts the zeros when multiplying or dividing multiples of 10, e.g. 40 × 50 = 200.
Misses factors by not working in pairs, e.g. leaves out 1 and the number itself, or one of a pair.
Mixes up factors and multiples.
Thinks every odd number is prime, e.g. 9, 21 or 51.
Thinks 1 is a prime number, or that 2 is not.
Multiplies by 2 to square a number, or by 3 to cube it, e.g. 6² = 12.
Names parts as halves, thirds or quarters when the parts are not equal.
Writes shaded parts over unshaded parts instead of over all the parts, e.g. 1 of 4 shaded as 1/3.
Thinks a bigger denominator means a bigger fraction, e.g. 1/8 > 1/3.
Finds one part of an amount but forgets to multiply by the numerator, e.g. 3/4 of 20 = 5.
Divides an amount by the numerator instead of the denominator, e.g. 2/5 of 30 = 15.
Makes an equivalent fraction by adding the same number to the numerator and denominator, e.g. 2/3 = 4/5.
Counts on past 0.9 as 0.10, or past 9/10 as 10/10 written 0.10, instead of reaching 1.
Puts the digits in the wrong decimal place, e.g. 7/100 written as 0.7.
Writes a fraction as a decimal using its digits, e.g. 1/4 = 0.4 or 1/5 = 0.15.
Compares fractions with different denominators by their numerators only, e.g. 3/8 > 2/3.
Converts between mixed numbers and improper fractions wrongly, e.g. 2 3/4 = 10/4 (multiplying the whole number by the numerator and adding the denominator).
Multiplies both the numerator and the denominator by a whole number, e.g. 3 × 2/5 = 6/15.
Thinks multiplying always makes a number bigger, so a product of proper fractions must be bigger than both.
Multiplies the numerator instead of dividing when dividing a fraction by a whole number, e.g. 1/3 ÷ 2 = 2/3.
Converts between percentages, fractions and decimals by copying digits, e.g. 7% = 0.7 or 1/4 = 4%.
Uses an additive relationship where the relationship is multiplicative, e.g. 3 makes 6 so 5 makes 8.
Finds a percentage of an amount by dividing by the percentage, e.g. 15% of 360 = 360 ÷ 15.
Shares in a ratio by dividing by one part or by the number of terms instead of the total number of parts.
Writes a ratio in the wrong order.
Simplifies a ratio by subtracting the same number from both parts, e.g. 6:9 = 4:7.
Mixes up part:part and part:whole, e.g. reads 2:3 as two thirds of the whole.
Multiplies when it should divide when converting units, or the reverse, or uses the wrong factor.
Uses the length conversion factor for area or volume, e.g. 1 m² = 100 cm².
Writes one quantity as a fraction of another without first making the units the same, e.g. 30 cm of 2 m is 30/2.
Uses the percentage alone as the multiplier for a percentage change, e.g. × 0.15 for a 15% increase.
Finds an original value by taking the percentage off the new value, e.g. after a 20% rise to 60, gives 60 − 12 = 48.
Combines the quantities the wrong way in a compound measure, e.g. speed = distance × time.
Treats inverse proportion as direct, e.g. thinks more workers take more days.
Uses the length scale factor for areas or volumes of similar shapes instead of its square or cube.
Treats repeated percentage change as simple, e.g. adds 3 × 5% for three years of 5% compound interest.
Works out a percentage change by dividing by the new value instead of the original value.
Reads a value from a graph as the rate of change, instead of working out the change in y divided by the change in x.
Thinks any straight-line graph shows direct proportion, even one that does not pass through the origin.
Reads 3y or ab as addition or as digits side by side, e.g. if y = 4 then 3y = 34 or 7.
Squares a negative number to get a negative, e.g. (−3)² = −9, or squares only the digit.
Mixes up expression, equation, formula, inequality and identity.
Collects unlike terms together, e.g. 3a + 2b = 5ab.
Multiplies only the first term in a bracket, e.g. 3(x + 4) = 3x + 4.
Gets a position-to-term rule wrong by ignoring the first term or using the difference as the constant, e.g. 5, 8, 11 as 3n or n + 3.
Uses the wrong inverse operation, or applies it to only one side, when solving or rearranging, e.g. x + 5 = 12 gives x = 17.
Multiplies only the first terms and the last terms when expanding two brackets, e.g. (x + 2)(x + 3) = x² + 6.
Reads or plots coordinates the wrong way round, as (y, x).
Works out a gradient as horizontal change over vertical change, or ignores its sign.
Mixes up the gradient and the intercept in y = mx + c.
Chooses a factor pair with the right product but the wrong sum or signs when factorising x² + bx + c.
Multiplies the powers when multiplying terms with the same base, e.g. a² × a³ = a⁶.
Adds the equations when it should subtract to eliminate a variable, or the reverse.
Treats a geometric sequence as arithmetic, adding a difference instead of multiplying by a ratio.
Does not reverse the inequality when multiplying or dividing by a negative number, or uses the wrong circle on a number line.
Multiplies out a bracket after a minus sign without changing every sign inside, e.g. −2(x − 4) = −2x − 8.
Undoes the operations in the wrong order when changing the subject, e.g. y = mx + c gives x = y ÷ m − c.
Confuses an equation, true for particular values, with an identity, true for every value.
Applies the steps of a function or function machine in the wrong order, or reverses it without reversing the order.
Finds a midpoint by halving the difference of the coordinates instead of averaging them.
Confuses the roots, the turning point and the y-intercept of a quadratic graph.
Matches an equation to the wrong type of graph, e.g. thinks y = x³ is a parabola or y = 1/x is a straight line.
Misreads a distance–time graph, e.g. thinks a horizontal section means moving at a steady speed or a steeper line means slower.
Gives the solutions of (x − a)(x − b) = 0 with the wrong signs, e.g. x = −a.
Gives only the positive solution of a quadratic, e.g. x² = 9 gives only x = 3.
Writes a situation in algebra in the wrong order or with the wrong operation, e.g. "5 less than n" as 5 − n.
Names a sequence type wrongly, e.g. calls 1, 4, 9, 16 arithmetic or 2, 4, 8 linear.
Counts the symbols in a pictogram without using the key, e.g. reads 3 symbols as 3 when each stands for 2.
Misreads a chart scale, e.g. counts each grid line as 1 when the scale goes up in 2s, 5s or 10s.
Reads a pie chart sector angle as the frequency, or compares pie charts of different totals by angle alone.
Divides by the wrong number when finding a mean, e.g. leaves out a zero or divides by the number of rows in a frequency table.
Takes the middle value of the data without putting it in order first.
Gives the highest frequency instead of the value that has it as the mode.
Thinks a correlation shows that one variable causes the other.
Works with times as if they were decimals, with 100 minutes in an hour, e.g. 9:50 to 10:05 is 55 minutes.
Judges length, weight or capacity by how an object looks, e.g. thinks the taller container always holds more or the bigger object is always heavier.
Puts events, days or months in the wrong order, or mixes up words such as before, after, first and next.
Reads a scale on a jug, thermometer or weighing scales as if each mark were worth 1, without working out what each interval is worth.
Reads the number at the end of an object on a ruler without starting from 0 or taking away the starting reading.
Counts the coins rather than adding their values, or thinks a bigger coin is worth more, e.g. three coins make 3p.
Mixes pounds and pence, e.g. writes 250p as £25.0, £3.05 as 35p, or adds £1.50 and 75p to make £76.50.
Works out change wrongly by taking each digit from 10, e.g. change from £1 for 35p as 75p.
Mixes up the hour hand and the minute hand.
Reads the number the minute hand points to as the minutes, e.g. reads 20 past as 4 past because the hand points to 4.
Reads the hour the hour hand is nearest to rather than the one it has passed, e.g. reads 2:50 as 3:50.
Confuses past and to, e.g. reads quarter to 4 as quarter past 4, or counts minutes to the hour from the wrong hour.
Uses a wrong time fact, e.g. 100 minutes in an hour, 100 seconds in a minute, 12 hours in a day or 30 days in every month.
Converts between 12-hour and 24-hour times wrongly, e.g. writes 3 pm as 03:00 or 13:00, or reads 17:00 as 7 pm.
Adds, takes away or compares measures in different units without converting first, e.g. 1 kg + 300 g = 301 g.
Uses the wrong factor or the wrong operation to convert between metric units, e.g. 1 km = 100 m or 3 m = 0.03 cm.
Converts between metric and imperial units the wrong way round, e.g. says 10 inches is about 4 cm.
Confuses perimeter and area, e.g. counts the squares inside a shape when asked for its perimeter.
Adds only the labelled sides of a rectilinear shape, leaving out sides whose lengths have to be worked out.
Thinks shapes with the same area must have the same perimeter, or the reverse.
Multiplies base by height for a triangle without halving.
Uses a slanted side instead of the perpendicular height for the area of a parallelogram or triangle.
Adds the length, width and height of a cuboid instead of multiplying them, or counts only the cubes that can be seen.
Multiplies the sum of the parallel sides by the height without halving, or adds all four sides, for the area of a trapezium.
Confuses the formulae for the circumference and the area of a circle, e.g. uses πr² for the circumference or 2πr for the area.
Finds the surface area of a cuboid or prism from only the faces that can be seen, e.g. adds three faces of a cuboid instead of six.
Confuses surface area and volume, e.g. multiplies the three edges when asked for the surface area.
Continues a repeating pattern by copying the last item or the wrong group, rather than finding the part that repeats.
Mixes up odd and even numbers, e.g. says 7 is even, rather than checking whether it shares equally into two groups.
Doubles a number by adding 1 or 2 instead of adding the number to itself, e.g. says double 4 is 6.
Confuses opposite position words, e.g. on and under, in front of and behind, or before and after in a line.
Writes favourable over unfavourable outcomes instead of over all outcomes, e.g. 3 red and 5 blue gives P(red) = 3/5.
Places probability words in the wrong place on the 0 to 1 scale, e.g. calls 0.3 likely.
Expects results of an experiment to match the theoretical probability exactly, or thinks past results change the next outcome.
Finds the probability of something not happening wrongly, e.g. 1 − 0.35 = 0.75.
Counts the overlap of a Venn diagram twice, or leaves it out, when finding totals.
Treats outcomes such as the total of two dice as equally likely, e.g. thinks 7 and 2 are equally likely.
Moves a shape or point the wrong way in a translation, e.g. left instead of right, or applies the across and up amounts to the wrong coordinates.
Counts the empty squares between a shape and its image as the distance moved, rather than how far one vertex moves to its matching vertex.
Thinks a translation, reflection or rotation changes the size or shape of a figure.
Reflects in the other axis, e.g. changes the sign of x when reflecting in the x-axis.
Rotates about the wrong point, e.g. a vertex of the shape instead of the given centre.
Adds the scale factor to lengths or coordinates instead of multiplying, e.g. enlarges a 3 cm side by scale factor 2 to 5 cm.
Ignores the centre of enlargement, e.g. multiplies the coordinates by the scale factor as if the centre were the origin.
Uses 360° as the total for angles on a straight line, confusing it with angles at a point.
Uses 180° as the total for angles at a point, confusing it with angles on a straight line.
Adds the known angles together instead of subtracting them from the total.
Uses 360° as the total for the angles in a triangle.
Uses 180° as the total for the angles in a quadrilateral.
Thinks vertically opposite angles add up to 180° instead of being equal.
Judges the size of an angle by the length of its arms rather than the amount of turn.
Mixes up the names of angle types, for example calling an obtuse angle reflex or a reflex angle obtuse.
Names an angle with the vertex letter first or last instead of in the middle, so ∠ABC is read as the angle at A.
Reads the wrong scale of a protractor, giving 180° minus the angle.
Divides by the scale factor instead of multiplying when turning a scale drawing into real lengths (or the reverse).
Confuses clockwise with anticlockwise.
Confuses quarter, half and three-quarter turns, for example calling two right angles a quarter turn.
Mixes up parallel and perpendicular lines.
Thinks two lines are parallel just because they do not meet in the part that is drawn.
Thinks alternate or corresponding angles add up to 180° instead of being equal.
Thinks co-interior angles are equal instead of adding up to 180°.
Thinks opposite angles of a parallelogram add up to 180° instead of being equal.
Finds the total of a kite's two equal angles but forgets to share it between them.
Thinks a shape changes when it is turned, for example that a square standing on a corner is not a square.
Does not see that one shape can be a special case of another, for example that a square is a rectangle.
Counts the corners (vertices) of a shape when asked for its sides, or the reverse, or counts one side twice.
Takes the angle between the two equal sides of an isosceles triangle to be equal to the base angles.
Thinks the diagonals of a rectangle or parallelogram are lines of symmetry.
Slides half of a shape across the mirror line instead of reflecting it.
Gives the distance from a point to the mirror line when asked how far the point is from its reflection, which is twice as far.
Thinks a polygon is regular just because its sides are equal, ignoring its angles.
Uses n × 180° for the sum of the interior angles of an n-sided polygon instead of (n − 2) × 180°.
Confuses the interior and exterior angles of a polygon.
Thinks the diagonals of every rectangle meet at right angles, as they do in a square.
Thinks the diagonal of a rectangle cuts its corner angle in half, as it does in a square.
Finds a missing side from a rectangle's perimeter without allowing for there being two of each side, for example subtracting one length from the whole perimeter.
Confuses the radius and the diameter, for example halving when it should double.
Mixes up a sector (between two radii) and a segment (between a chord and an arc).
Thinks every chord is a diameter, or that a diameter is not a chord.
Halves instead of doubling: thinks the angle at the centre is half the angle at the circumference.
Forgets that a tangent meets the radius at a right angle.
Thinks opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are equal instead of adding up to 180°.
Thinks three equal angles (AAA) prove two triangles are congruent, when they only prove the triangles are similar.
Thinks two sides and an angle that is not between them (SSA) always prove two triangles are congruent.
Labels the side next to an angle with that angle's letter, instead of the side opposite it.
Thinks any three lengths make a triangle, without checking the two shorter sides add up to more than the longest.
Measures a bearing anticlockwise from north instead of clockwise.
Gives the same bearing for the return journey instead of adding or subtracting 180°.
Gives a correct number but the wrong reason, or a reason that does not justify the step.
Confuses the perpendicular bisector (points equidistant from two points) with the angle bisector (points equidistant from two lines).
Measures the distance from a point to a line along a slanted line instead of the perpendicular, which is the shortest.
Adds or subtracts the side lengths without squaring them, or forgets to take the square root at the end.
Adds the squares when finding a shorter side, so gets a length longer than the hypotenuse.
Chooses the wrong trigonometric ratio, e.g. uses sin with the opposite and adjacent sides.
Names a 3D shape with the name of a 2D shape, e.g. calls a cube a square or a sphere a circle.
Mixes up faces, edges and vertices when describing a 3D shape, e.g. says a cube has 8 edges.
Counts only the faces, edges or vertices that can be seen in a drawing of a 3D shape.
Names the wrong 2D shape for the faces of a 3D shape, e.g. thinks every face of a triangular prism is a triangle.
Confuses prisms and pyramids, e.g. thinks a pyramid has the same cross-section all the way through.
Thinks any six squares joined edge to edge will fold into a cube.
Thinks a shape with curved surfaces will stack steadily, or that a shape with only flat faces will roll.
Miscounts the smaller shapes that make up a shape, e.g. counts only the outline or misses some parts.
